mcqs.question: What does SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) mean?
options: Multiple independent threads each executing different instructions on different cores
One instruction applying the same operation to several data elements simultaneously, packed into a wide register
One instruction that can only operate on a single data element but runs faster than usual
A technique for scheduling instructions across multiple pipeline stages
mcqs.explanation: SIMD's defining property is a single instruction acting on multiple packed data elements at once, which is data parallelism within one instruction, not multiple threads on multiple cores (that's a different, thread-level parallelism model) and not merely a faster single-element operation.

mcqs.question: Why is a single SIMD add on a 128-bit register faster than four separate scalar add instructions computing the same four sums?
options: Because SIMD instructions run at a higher clock frequency than scalar instructions
Because the SIMD instruction is fetched, decoded, and issued once and processes all four elements in its lanes simultaneously, while the scalar version pays that overhead four separate times
Because scalar add instructions cannot use the ALU at all
Because SIMD instructions skip the memory hierarchy entirely
mcqs.explanation: The throughput gain comes from amortizing fetch/decode/issue overhead across all packed elements in one instruction rather than paying it four times over, not from a higher clock rate. Scalar adds absolutely use the ALU, and SIMD instructions still go through the normal memory hierarchy for their loads and stores.

mcqs.question: In the auto-vectorization example, what allows the compiler to turn a simple scalar loop into SIMD instructions without any special syntax from the programmer?
options: The compiler always assumes any loop can be vectorized regardless of dependencies
The compiler recognizes the loop iterations are independent of each other, so it can safely group multiple iterations into one wide SIMD instruction
The CPU itself detects scalar loops at runtime and rewrites them
Auto-vectorization requires the programmer to add a compiler pragma before it activates at any optimization level
mcqs.explanation: Auto-vectorization is a static compiler analysis that proves loop iterations don't depend on each other, allowing them to be safely batched into SIMD instructions — it does require that independence, it isn't assumed blindly. It happens at compile time, not by the CPU rewriting code at runtime, and many compilers vectorize automatically at standard optimization levels without requiring an explicit pragma.

mcqs.question: Why do loops with heavy per-element, data-dependent branching resist SIMD vectorization?
options: Because SIMD registers cannot hold integer values, only floating-point

Because SIMD requires all lanes to execute the same operation in lockstep, and different elements needing different code paths can't cleanly map onto one instruction without masking overhead or falling back to scalar
Because branches are not allowed anywhere in a program that uses SIMD
Because compilers cannot generate any code for loops containing an if statement
mcqs.explanation: SIMD's lockstep-per-lane execution model assumes uniform operations across elements; per-element branching breaks that assumption, forcing either masked execution of both paths (wasting work) or a scalar fallback. SIMD registers do hold integers, branches elsewhere in a program aren't forbidden, and compilers can generate code for loops with if statements — they just may not vectorize them well.
